title: field-playbook-speed-vs-cost
body:
Purpose:

This quick playbook gives SEs and AEs a compact set of claims, guardrails, and lightweight proof artifacts to use when arguing Redwood is the pragmatic choice for teams that care about both latency and per-token spend. Focused on chat-like and mixed-interaction workloads where we get the biggest wins.

One-sentence opener for discovery calls:

- "We help teams get predictable p99 latency and meaningfully lower per-token bills by combining runtime optimizations with routing and cache-aware serving — we can show you numbers from your traffic in 48 hours."

Elevator claims (short, conditional):

- Claim 1: "For interactive, multi-turn chat workloads, enabling Redwood caching + batching typically cuts effective per-token cost by roughly 25–55% vs unmanaged endpoints."
- Claim 2: "Redwood’s routing and fallback policies keep p99s stable under regional pressure — customers see fewer latency spikes during peak events."
- Guardrail: Always tie the claim to workload type (chat vs long-generation), model family, and whether quantization is enabled.

Quick soundbites for different audiences:

- Engineering lead: "We hand you the knobs — batch policies, cache TTLs, quantization profiles — and tie them to observed cost/accuracy tradeoffs."
- Product manager: "Lower inference burn means you can keep higher QPS or add features like more agents/semantic search without blowing budget."
- Platform owner: "Same API across hosted, dedicated, and private — you can validate in hosted, then pin and move to reserved capacity if needed."

Top proof points to carry (short list):

1) Internal benchmark snapshots (suitable for slide inclusion):
   - Interactive chat baseline: median 90–130ms, p99 200–300ms for 8–16-token replies on quantized medium models in hosted region under mixed load.
   - Batching benefit: effective throughput up to 2.5x on mixed short/medium sessions when dynamic batching is active.
   - Per-token spend: modeled 25–55% reduction on chat-heavy traces once prefix cache and int8 profiles enabled; gains decline as average response length > 600 tokens.

2) Anonymized field notes:
   - Marketplace assistant: after switching to reserved pools + tuned batching, the customer reduced reserved GPU need by ~30% while maintaining p95 targets.
   - Internal POC: replayed a customer chat trace and toggled cache only -> cache+batching -> cache+batching+quantization; measured incremental savings and latency changes after each step.

3) Customer-ready assets to show live:
   - 10-slide demo deck: baseline vs optimized playback with charts (latency percentile trends, cache-hit%, cost projection).
   - Demo harness: small script that replays 48h traces and outputs a one-page cost/latency delta.

How to structure a quick field POC (48–72h minimal plan):

1) Collect: share 24–72h of anonymized prompt traces + target SLOs and budget sensitivity.
2) Baseline: replay traces against the customers current endpoint (if allowed) or a comparable cloud endpoint and record latency percentiles and cost estimate.
3) Redwood run 1: enable hosted defaults (no cache) to get apples-to-apples latency baseline.
4) Redwood run 2: enable prefix cache + conservative batching (short batch timeout), record deltas.
5) Redwood run 3: add quantization profile that preserves accuracy on your validation prompts, produce final delta and recommendation (hosted -> dedicated -> private).

SE scripts / checklist items to run during POC:

- Replayer flags: preserve interarrival times, annotate session ids for cache grouping, export cache-hit-rate per prefix.
- Capture: p50/p95/p99, effective batch size distribution, GPU utilization, tokens generated, and estimated dollars/token using current reserved pricing.
- Deliverable: one-page PDF showing baseline, each optimization step, recommended next deployment mode, and estimated monthly saving at target QPS.

Competitive framing (how to tell the story):

- Managed single-endpoint vendors: they sell simplicity; we sell controllability. When your workload is chatty, handing you cache and batching controls plus route-based SLA choices yields real monthly savings and predictable tail latency.
- Pure self-hosted stacks: you get customization but also ops burden; Redwood abstracts the complexity (autoscaling, kernel selection, KV cache placement) while preserving the levers that drive unit economics.

Common buyer objections and suggested rebuttals:

- "Our workloads are long-form generation, so caching wont help." -> Acknowledge: caching is less effective; shift to talking about quantization, cheaper model routing for batched jobs, and cost-per-token vs model choice tradeoffs. Offer a replay that shows those gains.
- "Your numbers look optimistic." -> Offer transparent replay: we run your traces and show stepwise deltas; keep public claims conservative in copy.

Legal / compliance note for field:

- Dont promise fixed % savings in public marketing collateral without Legal sign-off. In field decks, use ranges and always call out workload assumptions.

Open actions (assign and close in two weeks):

- [Miguel Santos] create a 1-slide POC results template that SEs can populate and send to customers (due 2026-03-12).
- [Grace Li] publish the demo harness branch and include a quickstart README with example traces (due 2026-03-08).
- [Aisha Patel] finalize the internal benchmark snapshot file and register it in the SE toolkit (due 2026-03-10).

Quick field-ready lines to use verbatim:

- "We can baseline your traffic and show a stepwise cost/latency improvement in under 72 hours."
- "Typical chat-like customers see meaningful per-token savings when we enable cache and batching — exact numbers depend on your session lengths."

Status: draft for SE vetting. Keep this doc lean; move any lengthy methodology or CSVs to linked artifacts above.
